title: Strings, Unicode and indexing boundaries
outcome: Process text without confusing byte positions, Unicode characters and visible grapheme clusters.
key_terms: One byte of a UTF-8 `String`; `ncodeunits` counts them, and string indices are positions in this byte sequence.
One Unicode scalar value, stored in a `Char`, that can occupy between one and four UTF-8 code units.
The error raised when an index falls inside a multibyte character, which is why code steps with `nextind` or `eachindex`.
A user-perceived character, such as a letter plus a combining accent, that can span several code points.
Rewriting text to a canonical form such as NFC with `Unicode.normalize`, so composed and decomposed spellings compare equal.
approach: Keep three units apart: bytes indexed by `String`, characters returned by iteration, and graphemes a reader sees. Move between positions with `nextind` rather than `+ 1`, count with the function that matches the unit, normalize only by deliberate choice, and handle the empty string before asking for a first character.

exercises.title: Advance safely
exercises.task: Move from the first to the second character in the UTF-8 fixture.
exercises.answer: Adding one to a valid byte index can enter a multibyte character.
exercises.why: In `"éλ"` the letter é occupies bytes 1 and 2 in UTF-8, so `nextind("éλ", 1)` returns 3, where λ begins.
exercises.wrong: Using index 2 as the second character lands inside é, and `"éλ"[2]` throws `StringIndexError` instead of returning λ.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `nextind("éλ", 1) == 3`; also print `ncodeunits("éλ")`, which is 4, beside `length("éλ")`, which is 2.

exercises.title: Count visible units
exercises.task: Compare characters and graphemes in the combining-accent example.
exercises.answer: A visible text unit can contain multiple code points.
exercises.why: `"e\u0301"` stores e followed by a combining acute accent: two characters that render as one visible grapheme.
exercises.wrong: Reporting `length` as the visible count says 2 for a single displayed letter, which miscounts any text with combining marks.
exercises.verify: Compare `length(s)` with `length(collect(Unicode.graphemes(s)))` after `using Unicode`; expect 2 and 1.

exercises.title: Normalize deliberately
exercises.task: Apply NFC to the combining-accent fixture.
exercises.hint: Retain the original if exact provenance matters.
exercises.answer: Canonical equivalence is a specific Unicode relation, not arbitrary semantic equivalence.
exercises.why: NFC composes e plus U+0301 into the single code point U+00E9, so the normalized string equals the precomposed é.
exercises.wrong: Comparing the raw strings with `==` reports them unequal and could lead to duplicate keys for what readers consider the same word.
exercises.verify: Assert `Unicode.normalize("e\u0301", :NFC) == "\u00e9"` and keep the original string if provenance must be exact.

exercises.title: Handle empty text
exercises.task: Check an empty string before selecting its first character.
exercises.expected: The empty case is identified explicitly.
exercises.hint: Do not assume every string has index 1.
exercises.answer: A parser or display routine needs a documented empty-input policy.
exercises.why: `""` has no characters, so `first("")` fails; testing `isempty` first lets the routine apply its stated empty policy.
exercises.wrong: Assuming index 1 always exists produces an indexing error deep inside a parser rather than a clear message about empty input.
exercises.verify: The reference checks `isempty("")`; add a branch that returns `nothing` for empty input and test both branches.

exercises.title: Choose offset units
exercises.task: Store offsets for a cited text passage.
exercises.expected: Name byte, character or grapheme units and the text version.
exercises.hint: The source representation determines valid boundaries.
exercises.answer: Offsets are only reproducible against the same representation and indexing contract.
exercises.why: Citation offsets depend on the unit, since the same passage starting after é sits at byte 3 but character 2.
exercises.wrong: Storing bare integers without naming the unit lets a reader slice bytes with character counts and cut a character in half.
exercises.verify: Record each offset with its unit and text version, then reslice with `nextind` or `thisind` and confirm the cited text reappears.

exercises.title: Add a counterexample
exercises.task: Test an ASCII indexing algorithm with multibyte text.
exercises.expected: The invalid byte-index assumption becomes visible.
exercises.hint: Use an expected failure rather than silently deleting characters.
exercises.answer: A representative boundary fixture checks a mechanism that ASCII alone cannot exercise.
exercises.why: An algorithm that steps by `i + 1` works on `"ASCII"` because there `ncodeunits` equals `length`; multibyte text breaks that equality.
exercises.wrong: Testing only with ASCII fixtures passes every case while the byte-stepping bug remains, since every character there is one byte.
exercises.verify: Keep `ncodeunits("ASCII") == length("ASCII")` as the reference does, and add `@test_throws StringIndexError "éλ"[2]` as the counterexample.

checks_note: These six lines separate characters from bytes. `nextind("éλ", 1) == 3` holds because é occupies two code units, so the next valid index skips index 2. The ASCII comparison then shows the one case where `length` and `ncodeunits` agree. `join` and `string` build text without manual spacing, and `lowercase` normalizes a label without changing its meaning. If an edit makes `nextind` return 2, it is treating byte offsets as character positions.
